title: DeepBlip: Treatment Effects Unfolded
one_liner: A neural method that learns what each treatment dose does at each time step by flipping the usual sequential math on its head.
lead: In medicine, a patient takes many doses of a drug over weeks or months, and each dose nudges them a little closer to health. The question is: how much does dose three contribute, separate from doses one and two? DeepBlip answers this by building a neural model that learns the effect of each individual dose — called the blip effect — without the math constraint that usually forces you to learn them one at a time in sequence.

problem.h2: Why sequential learning is a dead end
paras: Imagine a doctor prescribing three doses of medicine over three months. To improve treatment for the next patient, we need to know: how much did dose one help, dose two, and dose three individually? The math framework that answers this — called structural nested mean models — works by learning the effect of dose three first, then using that answer to learn dose two, then dose one. It is locked into this backward-sequential order.

A beginner would try to build a neural network to learn all three effects at once using the standard gradient-based training (the same way you train any modern AI model). But the math constraint — the sequential g-estimation scheme — forbids this. The backward chain breaks if you try to optimize all three together, because the math for dose two depends on the answer for dose three. So neural approaches do not exist; researchers are stuck using older, slower methods that cannot capture complex patterns in time.

callout.html: Neural networks cannot learn time-specific treatment effects because the math that estimates them is inherently sequential.

paras: DeepBlip changes the learning order. Instead of learning time-step three, then two, then one — a sequence baked into the math — it learns all three together. It does this by introducing a double optimization trick: a clever rewriting of the loss function that lets you optimize all blip effects simultaneously while still getting mathematically correct answers.

hidden.h2: Blip effect: the time-specific dose contribution
hidden.name: Blip effect at time t
paras: A blip effect is the amount of health gain (or loss) from a single dose at a single moment in time, separated from all other doses. If a patient takes dose A in month one and dose B in month two, the blip effect of A is: the health change from A alone, as if B had not happened.

DeepBlip estimates this by training a neural network to predict blip effects, then extracting them. Instead of computing blips one-by-one in a backward sequence, the double optimization trick lets the network learn all of them at once, then reconstruct each one from the trained model.

heat.caption: Darker cells are blip effects and outcome shifts. Lighter cells are confounders (alternate explanations that must be ruled out).

reads.html: The blip is the true effect of one dose at one time, isolated from everything else.
In the structural nested mean model, the blip function gives the expected outcome change from an action at a given time, conditioned on all previous doses and health measurements.

mechanism.h2: Why the double optimization trick works
paras: The classical g-estimation forces you to learn blips backward because the math equation chains backward: to know dose three's effect, you first estimate dose three's outcome, then subtract it to isolate doses one and two, then repeat. This backward chain is unavoidable in pen-and-paper algebra.

DeepBlip's insight: rewrite the loss function as two nested optimization problems that can be solved simultaneously. One inner optimization solves for the confounding adjustment (the bias from sicker patients getting higher doses), and one outer optimization solves for the blip effects. By coupling these two optimizations in the right way, the loss becomes differentiable for all time steps at once. This lets a neural network learn all blips in parallel, using standard backpropagation, then extract each blip from the trained weights.

math.words: Total loss = (predicted outcome minus actual outcome) squared, plus a penalty for deviating from the unconfounded treatment assignment model.
math.equation: L = sum_i (Y_i - f(A_i, H_i))^2 + lambda * sum_i (g_hat(t_i, A_i) - g(A_i))^2
symbols: neural network predicting outcome from treatment history A and covariate history H
estimated confounding: probability of treatment A given history H at time t
the blip function: isolated effect of treatment A
weight balancing outcome prediction and confounding adjustment

worked.title: A tiny worked example with three doses
lines: Patient 1: took doses (low, med, high), final health 72 (measured).
Confounding model says: given health trend, probability of high dose should be 0.5, network assigns 0.4.
Total loss: 4.0 + lambda * 0.01. If lambda = 10, total is 4.1.
Backprop nudges both the outcome network and the blip functions to lower this loss next step.
After training, read the learned blip values to see each dose's isolated effect.

math.note: The trick: the two terms (outcome + confounding) are learned together in one backprop pass, not sequentially, so all time steps can be optimized in parallel.

bars.h2: Comparison with the old sequential method

charts.title: Sequential g-estimation (old way)
charts.note: Accurate at time 1 (learned last), but time 2 and 3 accumulate error. Sequential dependencies slow training.

charts.title: DeepBlip (parallel learning)
charts.note: DeepBlip learns all three at once using neural networks and backpropagation, producing more balanced accuracy because all time steps contribute equally to the loss, and faster training because there is no sequential dependency chain that must run one step at a time.

items.html: If a variable (like disease severity at baseline) affects both dose and outcome but is not recorded, DeepBlip cannot adjust for it. No method can; the data is simply incomplete.
If the rule for prescribing a dose changes mid-trial in an unexpected way, the model trained on the old pattern will estimate wrong blips.
The confounding adjustment model must be correctly specified. DeepBlip's Neyman-orthogonal loss reduces sensitivity to this, but not to zero.
With enough patient data and careful confounding adjustment, blip effects become unbiased and trustworthy.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic clinical trial: patients receive three doses of a drug over three time steps, each affecting their health score. Include time-varying confounding: sicker patients tend to receive higher doses at each step. Train DeepBlip on 1000 synthetic patients. Compare: (1) the blip effects the network learns versus (2) the ground-truth blip values you baked into the synthetic data. The metric is how close the estimates are. Also compare training time for DeepBlip (parallel) versus sequential g-estimation (sequential).
demo.closing: The demo should make two things impossible to miss: DeepBlip recovers the true time-specific dose effects despite time-varying confounding (because the double optimization balances outcome prediction with confounding adjustment), and it does so much faster than the old sequential method (because neural backpropagation learns all time steps in parallel rather than one at a time).
